# Model 4 (See What Sticks)

Because the numeric only model proved to be a good reduction, but the categorical was just a slight improvement on the base model, I added in everything to then move forward in future models through subtraction. Throwing everything at the wall here resulted in the best RMSE so far.

```{python}
#| warning: false

import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

data = pd.read_csv('../PACFiles/analysis_data.csv')
# Encode categorical variables as demonstrated in our class guides
X = pd.get_dummies(data.drop(['customer_id', 'monthly_spend'], axis=1), drop_first=True).fillna(0)
y = data.monthly_spend

reg = LinearRegression()
reg.fit(X,y)

scoring_data = pd.read_csv('../PACFiles/scoring_data.csv')
scoring_X = pd.get_dummies(scoring_data.drop(['customer_id'], axis=1), drop_first=True).fillna(0)
# Aligning columns between training and scoring data
scoring_X = scoring_X.reindex(columns=X.columns, fill_value=0)
pred = reg.predict(scoring_X)

submission_file = pd.DataFrame({'customer_id': scoring_data.customer_id, 'monthly_spend': pred})
submission_file.to_csv('../PACFiles/submission_file_5.csv', index=False)

from sklearn.metrics import root_mean_squared_error
train_pred = reg.predict(X)
rmse = root_mean_squared_error(y, train_pred)
print("Training RMSE:", rmse)
```
